Findings In this systematic review and meta-analysis of 63 cohort studies comprising 109 341 participants, although more severely ill patients received clozapine, use of clozapine was associated with better effectiveness outcomes regarding hospitalization, all-cause discontinuation, and overall symptoms but with a higher risk of cardiometabolic-related outcomes vs other SGAs. Meaning In a more generalizable sample of patients with schizophrenia than in randomized trials, clozapine was statistically and clinically associated with better effectiveness outcomes compared with other SGAs, but some concerns about safety require careful monitoring and clinical attention. ---------------------------------------- This systematic review and meta-analysis compares various outcomes of clozapine vs oral nonclozapine second-generation antipsychotics in cohort studies of patients with schizophrenia. Abstract Importance Recent meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing clozapine with nonclozapine second-generation antipsychotics (NC-SGAs) in schizophrenia have challenged clozapine’s superiority in treatment-resistant patients. However, patients in RCTs are not necessarily generalizable to those in clinical practice. Objective To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare various outcomes of clozapine vs oral NC-SGAs in cohort studies. Data Sources Systematic literature search in PubMed, PsycINFO, and CINAHL without language restriction from database inception until December 17, 2018. Study Selection Nonrandomized cohort studies reporting effectiveness and/or safety outcomes comparing clozapine with NC-SGAs in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Data Extraction and Synthesis Independent investigators assessed studies and extracted data. Using a random-effects model, the study calculated risk ratio (RR) unadjusted for covariates and follow-up duration, number needed to treat/number needed to harm (NNT/NNH) for dichotomous data, and standardized mean difference (SMD) or mean difference (MD) for continuous data. Main Outcomes and Measures Coprimary outcomes were hospitalization and all-cause discontinuation. Secondary outcomes included all effectiveness and safety outcomes reported in at least 3 analyzable studies. Results Of 8446 hits, 68 articles from 63 individual cohort studies (n = 109 341) (60.3% male; mean [SD] age of 38.8 [6.5] years, illness duration of 11.0 [5.1] years, and study duration of 19.1 [23.3] months) were meta-analyzed. Compared with NC-SGAs, despite greater illness severity (17 studies [n = 38 766]; Hedges g, 0.222; 95% CI, 0.013-0.430; P = .04), clozapine was significantly associated with lower hospitalization risk (19 studies [n = 49 453]; RR, 0.817; 95% CI, 0.725-0.920; P = .001; NNT, 18; 95% CI, 12-40) and all-cause discontinuation (16 studies [n = 56 368]; RR, 0.732; 95% CI, 0.639-0.838; P < .001; NNT, 8; 95% CI, 6-12). Associations were statistically significant for comparisons with quetiapine fumarate and aripiprazole regarding hospitalization and all NC-SGAs, except aripiprazole, for all-cause discontinuation. Clozapine was also significantly associated with better outcomes regarding overall symptoms (SMD, −0.302; 95% CI, −0.572 to −0.032; P = .03) and Clinical Global Impressions scale severity (SMD, −1.182; 95% CI, −2.243 to −0.122; P = .03). Clozapine was significantly associated with increases in body weight (MD, 1.70; 95% CI, 0.31-3.08 kg; P = .02), body mass index (MD, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.24-1.68; P = .009), and type 2 diabetes (RR, 1.777; 95% CI, 1.229-2.570; P = .002; NNH, 27; 95% CI, 13-90). fetched_contents.text: A 20-Year Population-Based Follow-Up Study on the Association Between Clozapine and Hospitalization in People With Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia Schizophrenia affects approximately 24 million individuals globally and is characterized by significant functional impairment, frequent relapses, and a lifelong risk of disability (1). Approximately 15% to 30% of patients with schizophrenia do not respond adequately to standard antipsychotic treatments and are considered to have treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) (2,3). Patients with TRS have even poorer outcomes (2) and 3- to 11-fold higher direct health care costs than the whole schizophrenia population, mostly attributable to higher rates of hospitalization (4). Clozapine is the only medication approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of TRS (5). Because of its side-effect profile, clozapine has been considered only as a third-line treatment for schizophrenia, specifically for TRS in most developed countries and regions, including Hong Kong (6). Although symptomatic improvement is the primary outcome in clozapine efficacy studies for TRS in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), reductions in hospitalization may also indicate clinical benefit. A network meta-analysis (7) and a recent individual patient data meta-analysis (8) of RCTs have not shown clozapine to be superior to other second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) in improving symptoms of patients with TRS. In contrast, 2 meta-analyses suggested possible superiority of clozapine in reducing hospitalizations (9), which could reflect its clinical effectiveness. However, limitations of these studies restricted the interpretation of their results. Most studies employed a cohort design; thus, the differences in group compatibility and the presence of confounding factors may have introduced bias into the results. Additionally, these studies tend to include patients with general schizophrenia diagnoses or varied psychiatric diagnoses, instead of TRS. Of 37 studies in one meta-analysis, only 12 studies focused on TRS (10). Furthermore, studies tend to examine hospitalization in general without separating psychiatric and non-psychiatric hospitalizations and without considering other environmental factors such as seasonality and infectious outbreaks (11). Health care system differences, including integrated community psychiatric services and early intervention services and psychiatric bed availability (11,12), may also impact hospitalization rates. Most of the existing literature is from the West and thus is difficult to generalize to different populations and health care contexts. There is substantial evidence on the effect of long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIAs) in reducing hospitalization and rehospitalization in patients with schizophrenia (13). Recent studies have also suggested the potential role of LAIAs, both as monotherapy and in combination with clozapine, in the treatment of patients with TRS, including reduction of hospitalization (14). However, evidence of the effectiveness of LAIAs in TRS compared with clozapine is still limited. Additionally, due to inherent individual differences, previous cohort studies have been unable to adequately assess the comparative effectiveness of clozapine, LAIAs, and their combined use. To address the limitations of traditional epidemiological cohort study designs in studying real-world pharmacological effectiveness using large health care databases, self-controlled study designs have been advocated, including the self-controlled case series (SCCS) design (15). The SCCS design enables the study of recurrent outcomes over the entire observation period within the same individuals, so that the individuals serve as their own comparator, thus controlling for within-subject stable and time-varying confounding factors. Time-varying contextual factors could be adjusted as confounders in the SCCS model. Applying this model in studying the impact of clozapine on hospitalization using large health care databases may fill the gaps in existing literature, particularly the differential impact of clozapine on specific types of hospitalization risk, as well as the lack of robust comparisons between clozapine and LAIAs. The current study aimed to examine the association of clozapine with hospitalization for over a 20-year period in a population-representative cohort of patients with TRS compared with other antipsychotics using the SCCS design in Hong Kong, considering important time-varying contextual information. Comparison of clozapine and LAIAs on the reduction of hospitalization in this population was also studied. The CDARS is an electronic health record (EHR) repository maintained by the Hong Kong Hospital Authority, which serves more than 7.4 million people and provides approximately 90% of psychiatric care for severe mental illness, supplying reliable information on medication use and mortality (16). This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster (UW 20-854). Reporting adhered to the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines (17). fetched_contents.text: Biological Predictors of Clozapine Response: A Systematic Review Abstract Background: Clozapine is the recommended antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) but there is significant variability between patients in the degree to which clozapine will improve symptoms. The biological basis of this variability is unknown. Although clozapine has efficacy in TRS, it can elicit adverse effects and initiation is often delayed. Identification of predictive biomarkers of clozapine response may aid initiation of clozapine treatment, as well as understanding of its mechanism of action. In this article we systematically review prospective or genetic studies of biological predictors of response to clozapine.
